utterances.text: All right. Good evening, council. It's good to be back in these chambers. I had the pleasure of serving for the City of Centerfall for several years before I went over to the county. So it's particularly exciting to get to work on an issue that is certainly cross jurisdictional here in Marin county when it comes to public safety, especially youth on moving bikes. That is something that, of course, we know the best solution is going to be one that is across Marin's jurisdictional boundaries. So this evening I have, I'm going to keep it relatively short, a presentation for you all just covering the history of E bike safety here in Marin and particularly with the youngest riders here in Marin that is really the target of our efforts here at the county and of course at the various city levels. And talk about what you are considering tonight, which is going to be an ordinance that is in alignment with Assembly Bill 1778 last year. And then I'll talk also about next steps. All right, so I just want to start with some background. So as you all know, I really want to start by framing that Marin has long been a very enthusiastic supporter of active transportation. I think it's no accident that we saw the rise of E bikes and their use here in Marin county ahead of other areas in the state, just as Marin saw the rise of mountain bikes and other types of bikes. We are early adopters and we are proud early adopters and enthusiasts, as I noted, of active transportation. So that being said, you know where we are today. This really actually started with our EMS data. So our public health partners and 911 responders noted between 2019 and 2022, a twofold increase, 110% in the number of 911 accidents that involved bicycles and riders under 16. So the 10 to 15 year old age group at the time, we, like every other jurisdiction, were not differentiating between whether these involved a conventional bicycle or an E bike. And so our public health officer at the time, Dr. Matt Willis, worked with EMS responders across Marin county to actually start tracking that data. Are these involving an E bike or are these involving a conventional bike? And what we saw pretty quickly and consistently to today since 2023 is that for conventional bikes, 10 to 15 year olds have an accident, 911 accidents. This is a very serious accident rate that's about one and a half times as high as any other age group. But for e bikes, 10 to 15 year olds have an accident rate that is actually five times higher. And since E bikes are far less prevalent in the community, what that tells us is that E bikes are significant, have a significantly higher injury risk for the youngest riders for this 10 to 15 year old age group. I also just want to note that, you know, we can give you the statistics and we continue to publish them monthly on a dashboard that Marin HHS maintains. But really what drove a lot of this policy change was actually activists from Marin's emergency rooms and physicians that were treating some of the young patients and seeing the injuries that they were coming in from E bike accidents. These were injuries that were much more akin to motor vehicle accidents than we had seen typically with conventional bicycles. So on that note, I just want to show this quick graphic here and I invite you to check out our data dashboard that is maintained by our amazing public health team. But. But what I just want to draw your attention to is if you look at the blue lines across the different age groups, it is higher for 10 to 15 to 10 to 15 year olds, but not dramatically higher. As you see the orange bars, the orange bars, you're going to see an accident rate for 10 to 15 year olds that is five times higher. So I just want to now bring this around to what we're considering tonight. So, of course, I have to start with describing the three types of legal E bike classifications in California. I do want to note this is California law. Different states may have different classifications or definitions. So In California, Class 1 and Class 2 have motor that assists up to 20 miles an hour. The difference is Class 1 is pedal assisted, and Class 2, you can actually use a throttle for the motor to assist you. Class 3E bikes in California are legally pedal assist only. However, they are already in California law restricted to rider six seen and up. And that's because they go up to 28 miles an hour. So I do want to note class one and two, the motor can only assist up to 20 miles an hour. If you're thinking, hey, I've been driving down Point San Pedro and I've seen an ebike pass me, and I know I was going 20 miles an hour. What we have seen is there, there have been a number of cases where young folks have, you know, Jerry rigged Class 2 throttle ebikes to actually go past illegal speed. And I just want to point that out because we do know that that is out there. But again, we see this with the Class 2 throttle E bikes, not so much with the pedal assist, because you can't actually jerry rig those. All right, so I just want to note a few local actions here to that we have taken in Marin since really tracking this data and seeing where the issue is coming from. So I want to note that really starting a year and a half ago, Supervisor Mary Sackett and myself, we started engaging with the Federal Consumer Product Safety Commission. And the reason is because as I noted these are three legal E bike classifications in California, but you can purchase an E bike online that is not street legal in California. And why? That's because E bikes are regulated like bicycles from the Consumer Product Safety Commission. And those are regulated per federal standards, not state by state law. And so we did know that there was really advocacy that was needed at the federal level to encourage movement towards, you know, age appropriate restrictions and also ensuring bikes are made in a way that you can't, for instance, you know, makeshift the motor to go faster than what the legal speed is supposed to be. That being said, currently federal efforts are a bit stagnated on the state level. I should note that really what this has come to is last year, Assemblymember Connolly's Bill, Assembly Bill 1778, which I will describe in the next slide before you. And what that bill did was offer Marin jurisdictions the opportunity to impose new age restrictions on Class 2 throttle E bikes, in addition to the statewide restrictions that we already see on Class 3, which is 16 and up. I want to note there was a grand jury report last year that you all responded to, in addition to other Marin cities and towns. And then I want to note that we convened a new special committee on youth E bike safety. I want to thank council member Kurtz for serving on that committee. And that was a cross, not only city, county, jurisdictional partnership, but we had school partnerships on there. Of course, we had law enforcement, we had the transportation authority of Marin, we had bike shop owners. And we really tried to bring together this group to look at what does Marin need to really adequately start to address and tackle this issue. And so the committee really came up, you know, kind of with two charges. One was to implement a countywide safety campaign. We decided we really wanted something that really spoke to Marin and again went across jurisdictional boundaries, but was really clear messaging and really could target teens. The other was, if we are considering these new rules under Assembly Bill 1778, Marin is just too small of a county to have a patchwork of laws, and we needed consistent messaging across all jurisdictions. All right, so what is Assembly Bill 1778? So this was signed into law about one year ago from our Marin county assembly member, Damon. So I want to note right here on the right hand side of this graph, it shows you what the 1778 ordinance would do and how it changes state law. I want to note that really this ordinance just targets Class 2 throttle E bikes. And what it does is it essentially regulates them the same way that Class 3e bikes already are in California. So it puts a 16 plus age limit on those throttle E bikes and requires riders of all ages to wear helmets. So I just want to note in terms of some of the coordination that we've done, I already described the work of the special committee. Of course we have been providing support to cities and towns who are considering these adoption, adopting these ordinances with their staff materials as well as just informational updates to city staff. And then I also want to note that we're going to focus on the next slide. But really a big piece of this was we knew that enforcement alone is just truly not the answer when we're talking about something that is truly behavior change and trying to get young riders to really treat these E bikes as, you know, fast moving vehicles that they're riding alongside cars in traffic. And how do you get teenagers to really treat these as vehicles that they need to be paying more attention to staying safe and especially really paying attention to their surroundings and following the rules of the road. And so with that, that's when we put together and launched last spring the E Bikers Club. So what is the E Bikers Club? Our target audience was Marin teens and parents. We knew that if we were passing new rules, we wanted to make sure everybody was aware these again are Marin county only. And so our key messaging was youngest riders. If they are on an E bike, they should be on pedal assist. But you will see the content of our posters. We say or a conventional bike. Some of the youngest riders. It's really important that you become a skilled, comfortable, conventional bike rider before you get on an E bike. The other one was maintenance needs for E bikes. E bikes need more frequent brake replacement. You need to have a shop that will service your E bike. And so if you bought your bike online and a local shop won't service your E bike, then you have a problem. And safe riding tips, including of course, helmets. That's not new to bike safety, but tandem riding we have seen with some of these bikes. So making sure folks aren't are following traffic laws. Next slide. So we were actually able to launch this campaign in May. I invite you all to check out e-bikers club.com we were actually really, really thrilled with the outcome of the work. The goal of the campaign was to make it not look like a government campaign. What was actually helpful is we had some high schoolers and middle schoolers on our RFP panel which was a totally interesting experience. And really I thought it the the result was pretty awesome of of not only Marin landmarks, but a lot of them. Wanted the mascots from their middle schools and high schools incorporated. And as you can see in the video, again, we've really been incorporating Marin landmarks, making this a hyperlocal campaign to draw an attention. So timeline of key actions where we are at. So about a year ago, we convened our special committee. That committee kind of came up with its purpose in the spring. The county of Marin kind of led this charge, which is adopting the first Assembly Bill 1778 ordinance with a delayed implementation date of this summer. And actually now your council is going to be the final jurisdiction to consider this ordinance. So should your council adopt the ordinance, then all Marin cities and towns in addition to the county would have these ordinances to effect. We can continue with our consistent countywide messaging. And of course, back to school starts, I believe this week for many of the schools. And then finally, I just want to note measuring success. So how do we know this effort is going to be successful? We really started here because we had strong data, public health data, that told us that we had a real safety risk for some of our youngest residents and riders. So first and foremost, we are hoping that if this campaign and these new rules are successful in having fewer 10 to 15 year olds on throttle E bikes, which we have began tracking the class of E bike and you know, our public health team is going to kind of wait to publish that until we have enough data to publish. But we are seeing the vast majority of accidents do involve these throttle E bikes, bikes with youngest riders. We are hoping that that 911 injury and accident rate does go down.
